doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Ray Brown concert sparks switch to bass; borrowed tin bass
summary: Young Indianapolis musicians; Jazz at the Philharmonic makes him want bass, and he teaches himself on a friend's tin bass.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: My uncle didn’t tell me that, Eubie told me that, which is great. So playing music and then as I was a kid I was a part of a music club and all the young musicians around town like Freddie Hubbard, Virgil Jones, Mel Ryan and David Hardiman, on and on, we all came up playing jazz. And the Montgomery brothers, Wes, Buddy and Monk were there. And Monk befriended me, and it’s very interesting how as a young teenager — well first, how I came to play the bass was I went to a Jazz at the Philharmonic concert. And Ray Brown, Herb Ellis and Oscar Peterson and Ella Fitzgerald did a set that just totally knocked my socks off. And I said — because I’d been playing the violin — but I said that is what I want to do.
At about what year would it have been?
Oh God I can’t remember. I was about twelve or thirteen years old so I can’t do the math.
Somewhere around in there, yeah. Somewhere around in there. And I got a bass, and there was a friend of mine at the high school who had a bass, had one of those old tin © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
basses that they had, because they confiscated most of the wood and the plywood that the King Company were using to make basses. So they made these tin basses.

Black tin bass. And this guy came from a fairly well-to-do family and his parents just gave him everything. And he just had this bass. So I talked him into letting me borrow it for a while. And I taught myself how to play the bass.
